title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether integrating a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier with a bounded automated repair budget increases the fraction of intent‑driven network‑change proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high) using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Each paired intent produced one shared_initial generation reused for both conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (deterministic validation + ≤1 automated repair). Outcomes: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under the supplied synthetic suite and repair budget the single‑shot generator was near ceiling, limiting observable deterministic rescue. We archive preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts and interpret results with respect to estimand conditioning, validator coverage, repair budget, and operational deployment policies.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent→configuration translation, configuration synthesis, and automated repair. For pre‑deployment network changes, semantic correctness properties—sequencing constraints, reachability, and policy preservation—are operationally critical and cannot be assured by syntactic checks alone. A common engineering pattern pairs generative models with deterministic validators and bounded automated repair (generate→validate→repair) to reduce operational risk. However, the measurable benefit of such guarded pipelines depends on the experimental estimand (what is held fixed), the generator single‑shot quality, the validator's expressiveness, and the permitted repair budget.

We preregistered a paired experiment (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) to quantify the deterministic rescue achievable when the same single LLM candidate is evaluated under two treatments. For each intent the pipeline produced exactly one shared_initial candidate using the declared generator (gpt-5-mini) and compared: (a) baseline — accept the single candidate without repair, and (b) guarded — run a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and allow at most one automated repair which itself is re‑validated. The primary research question: does adding a deterministic verifier plus at most one automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation compared with accepting that same candidate without repair?

Our contributions: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation that isolates deterministic rescue under a shared_initial estimand; (2) a complete execution and analysis bundle including validator traces and the single automated repair transcript archived with the run; and (3) an evidence‑grounded interpretation of estimator conditioning, ceiling effects, and operational implications for NetOps pipelines.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and system reports document active use of LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, template synthesis, protocol testing, and repair) and the rise of tool‑augmented pipelines that let models call external validators or planners to improve reliability [1–4]. Planner‑centric and ReAct‑style frameworks have been proposed to coordinate multi‑tool workflows and reduce local decision traps [2]. Empirical work shows that introducing deterministic checks and generate→validate→repair scaffolds can improve correctness metrics relative to unconstrained generation, but gains depend on validator coverage, task distribution, and whether pipelines permit resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration [3–5]. Research on hallucination detection and deterministic safety nets supplies complementary mitigation techniques (semantic uncertainty, retrieval augmentation, self‑reflection) that are relevant to NetOps verification [6]. Finally, proposals for automatic configuration repair and hybrid symbolic/generative repair indicate potential but variable success depending on fault class and verifier expressiveness [4,7].

This study positions itself within these bodies of work by isolating the bounded, post‑generation verifier/repair effect (no resampling) and measuring deterministic rescue under an operationally meaningful model‑call budget.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The confirmatory design was preregistered (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001). The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded − baseline) on N = 300 paired intents under prespecified inclusion/exclusion rules. The preregistration fixed the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), the primary test (exact two‑sided McNemar), and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729, B = 10000). The preregistration described an optional calibration pilot (n = 60) for discordance estimation and power calibration; that pilot was not executed and no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed — this omission is stated here per the peer‑review requirement and affects achievable power for small absolute effects.

Task suite and sampling. Tasks were deterministically generated by the registered generator into a synthetic_topology suite stratified into difficulty strata (low/medium/high); confirmatory sampling used 100 paired intents per stratum. Representative difficulty patterns include 'shutdown_configure_restore' (medium) and 'paired_link_atomic_mtu_change' (hard). Difficulty composition observed in the archived run (all tasks considered) shows levels labeled extreme, very_hard, hard, and medium; detailed difficulty counts are archived with the execution bundle.

Shared_initial protocol, model, validator, and repair operator. To isolate deterministic validator/repair rescue from resampling effects we implemented the shared_initial estimand: for each pair the pipeline produced exactly one shared_initial candidate reused verbatim for both baseline and guarded conditions. The declared generator was gpt-5-mini (requested_model recorded in the model configuration). Semantic evaluation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing a full_intent_constraint_validation rule that deterministically checks sequencing invariants, preservation constraints, protected‑interface templates, and topology reachability encoded by the synthetic suite. The guarded pipeline allowed at most one automated repair attempt (repair budget ≤ 1); the repair operator was a constrained localized edit routine limited to sequencing/insert edits and applied only when the validator flagged the candidate. Repair attempts were re‑validated deterministically; repaired candidates that remained flagged counted as failures for guarded in the primary analysis.

Contamination, exclusions, and execution constraints. The preregistration included deterministic contamination controls and negative controls. Pairs would be excluded only if both pipeline calls failed due to provider/infrastructure outage; sensitivity analyses treat single-call failures as failures per the preregistered plan. The adapter enforced the pre‑specified model‑call budget and repair budget; execution instrumentation recorded model calls and stage counts for audit. All raw artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, repair traces, execution logs) are archived with the run bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary counts. The preregistered adapter completed the confirmatory run with complete_pair_count = 300 under the shared_initial protocol. Model‑call accounting shows model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared_initial generations + 1 repair invocation) and a single repair stage executed. Binary scoring produced baseline_success_count = 299 and guarded_success_count = 300, i.e., baseline = 299/300 (0.9966667) and guarded = 300/300 (1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Inferential results. The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test on the discordant counts returned p = 1.0. The absolute paired improvement (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729, B = 10000) is [0.00, 0.01]. With m = n10 + n01 = 1 discordant pair the exact test has limited sensitivity and the bootstrap CI bounds the plausible absolute improvement to at most one percentage point in this context.

Per‑stratum diagnostics and repair trace. Per the stratification, archived per‑stratum tallies were: low baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; medium baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; high baseline = 99/100 and guarded = 100/100. The solitary discordant pair occurred in the high stratum and invoked the allowed repair: the validator flagged a sequencing omission (missing 'admin down' before a VLAN/MTU change). The constrained repair operator inserted the missing sequencing command; the validator then reported valid == true. The repair produced a deterministic rescue at the cost of one additional repair stage call. All episode‑level validator before/after traces and the repair transcript are archived with the run bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

Contamination and missingness. Preplanned contamination checks and negative controls produced no contamination flags. No pairs were excluded under preregistered rules; there were zero failed or unscorable episodes in the confirmatory dataset.

Operational cost note. The guarded pipeline incurred one extra model/repair call across 300 pairs (model_calls_used = 301), indicating minimal additional model‑call cost for the single deterministic rescue observed on this synthetic suite.
sections.discussion:
Estimand and operational interpretation. The shared_initial estimand corresponds to policies that limit model calls (cost/latency/governance). Under that policy the guarded pipeline measures only deterministic validator and bounded repair rescue applied to the same candidate. Workflows that permit resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration change the estimand and typically raise achievable success rates by exploiting generator variance; such workflows require separate preregistered evaluation.

Ceiling effects and absent pilot. Baseline single‑shot performance was near ceiling (299/300) yielding minimal discordance (m = 1). The preregistration included an optional pilot (n = 60) to estimate discordance and calibrate power; that pilot was not executed and no post‑preregistration recalculation was performed. This practical omission reduced sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements and underlines the utility of small calibration pilots when generator performance may approach ceiling.

Validator coverage and repair budget. The single observed failure mode was a sequencing omission. The guarded pipeline's marginal utility depends on the distribution of failure modes in deployment and on validator expressiveness: richer validators detecting reachability or ACL semantics may yield higher rescue rates. The repair operator was intentionally constrained and limited to one localized edit; iterative repair or richer edit operators would address a different estimand and likely increase rescue opportunities.

Practical implications. For operational regimes that tightly bound model calls, the shared_initial estimand provides an informative bound on deterministic verifier/repair rescue. In this run bounded repair produced a deterministic rescue at negligible additional model cost, but the small absolute improvement reflects near‑ceiling baseline quality on the synthetic suite rather than a general guarantee.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study conditioning on one LLM draw per intent and allowing ≤1 constrained automated repair, baseline single‑shot generation (gpt-5-mini) produced 299/300 verifier‑unflagged proposals while the guarded pipeline produced 300/300, yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.00333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01]). Deterministic verifier+repair rescued a single sequencing omission at the cost of one additional repair call. The near‑ceiling baseline limits inferential power for small effects under the shared_initial estimand. We release the full preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts to enable targeted follow‑ups that vary estimand conditioning, repair budget, model strength, and task distributions.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated by the preregistered deterministic task generator; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase verifier marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing minimal discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements relative to larger pre‑specified targets.

Pilot not executed: the preregistered optional pilot intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed (reported and accounted for in Methods).

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (resampling or iterative generation).
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
